title: Sunny Orchard Row
story: A community garden has one long row of plots for fruit trees. From soil tests and sunlight, the gardeners know how many kilograms of fruit a tree would give in each plot. The catch: a tree crowds the roots of its neighbours, so two trees in plots right next to each other both do badly. So the gardeners never plant in two neighbouring plots.
If they choose the plots well, how much fruit can the row give?
task: Write maxHarvest(yields). yields[i] is the harvest in kilograms if plot i gets a tree. Choose any set of plots with no two neighbours (plots i and i + 1) both chosen, and return the largest possible total harvest.
You may leave plots empty. An empty row gives 0.

examples.explanation: Plant in plots 0 and 3: 6 + 9 = 15. Planting every other plot gives 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 or 2 + 9 = 11. The best choice leaves two plots in a row empty (plots 1 and 2), which the every-other pattern never does.
The best single plot is 7, but taking it blocks both neighbours. Taking the two 4s gives 8, which is more.

hints: Look at the last plot in [6, 2, 3, 9, 1]. In the best plan, either it has a tree or it does not. What does each case tell you about the rest of the row?

If the last plot is empty, the answer is the best plan for the row without it. If it has a tree, its neighbour must be empty, so the answer is its yield plus the best plan for the row without the last two plots.
Let best(i) be the most fruit from plots 0 to i. Then best(i) = max(best(i - 1), best(i - 2) + yields[i]). What are best for an empty row and for one plot?
Walk left to right keeping only two numbers: the best for the row up to the previous plot, and up to the plot before that. At each plot, compute the new best from those two and shift them along.
bruteForce: Try every subset of plots, skip the ones with two neighbours, and keep the best total. With 1,000 plots there are 2¹⁰⁰⁰ subsets, far too many. Even the valid ones grow exponentially.
Two shortcuts look tempting and are wrong. Taking every other plot fails on [6, 2, 3, 9, 1]. Grabbing the biggest yield first fails on [4, 7, 4].

js: * @param {number[]} yields  kilograms of fruit per plot
* @return {number} the largest total with no two neighbouring trees
let prev2 = 0; // best for the row up to two plots back
let prev1 = 0; // best for the row up to the previous plot
// skip this plot, or plant here and skip the neighbour
py: prev2 = 0  # best for the row up to two plots back
prev1 = 0  # best for the row up to the previous plot
# skip this plot, or plant here and skip the neighbour
walkthrough: Make one decision per plot, from left to right: plant or skip. If you skip plot i, you keep the best from plots before it. If you plant, plot i - 1 must be empty, so you add yields[i] to the best from two plots back. Take the larger.
• Plot 3 (9): max(9, 6 + 9) = 15. Planting here builds on the best up to plot 1, which was just plot 0.
Notice step 4: the plan it builds on skips both plot 1 and plot 2. The recurrence finds that on its own, because best already carries the right choice for every shorter row.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, constant work per plot.
solution.spaceWhy: Two running values instead of a full table.
solution.takeaway: For "pick items from a line, no two neighbours" problems, decide take-or-skip for the last item. Taking it jumps back two, skipping jumps back one, and the best of the two is the answer for this prefix.
